note: No para numbers (near end): challenge to Criminal Law (Amendment) Act 1969 s.6 amending CPC s.7 to let magistrates sentence under s.296 rejected: 'We can see no valid ground for assuming that the said amendment was contrary to the Constitution of Kenya.'

Mwera JA para 27 (not 42; majority strikes out appeal): s.75 CPA etc 'giving this Court jurisdiction ... should [not] be read to mean that these provisions of law also confer the right of appeal'; also headnote holding 4. One judge's reasoning in the majority.

Para 23-24: applies Mwaura precedent ('the Court affirmed that death sentence ... was the only lawful sentence'); sets aside HC's substituted sentence. Sentencing, not own holding on s.296 validity; HC sentence was not an event.

Para 26: sentencing 'in light of the emerging jurisprudence that even a life sentence ought to be determinate, we set aside the life imprisonment' - follows Kitsao/Maingi, no own reasoned holding on s.8(2).

Para 19-21: follows AWM and AOO ('The Courts have on previous occasions found that section 25(2) ... is unconstitutional'; 'we will not pretend to reinvent the wheel'); quote concerns the sentence, not a declaration on s.25(2).

Para 28: 'the issue regarding the constitutionality of the mandatory death sentence under Section 296 (2) ... is yet to be addressed as recommended by the Supreme Court' - court declines to adjudicate; restates Muruatetu 2 directions.

Para 10: 'we declare that the mandatory nature of the sentence of life imprisonment which was imposed on him by dint of section 8(2) ... is unconstitutional' - explicit declaration (drawing on Mwangi/Manyeso).
Para 25: 'we declare that the mandatory nature of the sentence of life imprisonment ... by dint of section 8(2) ... is unconstitutional' - explicit declaration, same formula as KECA 2024/327.

Para 38-40: challenge rejected but only by restating Muruatetu 2 and Simiyu: 'its applicability to defilement cases ... dealt a deathblow by the Supreme Court. The appellant's argument that the sentence imposed was unconstitutional ... is unfounded'. No own constitutional analysis.
Para 9-11: sole issue sentence; restates Muruatetu Directions and SC Mwangi: 'The implications of this clarification directly dispose the present appeal.' No own adjudication of s.296(2) validity.

Para 48-51: construes 'aged eleven years or less' in s.8(2): 'a child aged 11 years as contemplated under Section 8 (2) ... will only be 12 years a day preceding his twelfth birth day'. Real interpretation, but the quoted sentence ('properly sentenced') is the application, not the interpretive holding (that is in scope_text).
Para 153: 'we find sections 22 and 23 of the Act unconstitutional' - 'the Act' is the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018 (para 1), not KICA. Wrong Act.
Para 101: 'Section 5, as drafted, is therefore harmless and constitutional' (challenge also held premature) - s.5 of the Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.
Para 147: s.24(1)(c) 'the limitation is reasonable, proportional and justifiable' - Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.
Para 150: 'We thus find that the section is constitutionally sound' - s.27 Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.
Para 151: 'we reject the appellant's challenge to section 28 of the Act' (cybersquatting) - Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.
Para 131: s.50(2) 'the word "shall" is used in relation to the possible orders that a court can issue and not to command the court' - Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.
Para 132: s.52 six-month traffic data collection 'does not of itself render the provision unconstitutional' - Computer Misuse and Cybercrimes Act 2018, not KICA.

Issues para 1 & end: 'whether section 17 Cap. 234 is ultra vires' ... 'we do declare sub-section 17 [2] of the Act, unconstitutional' - Cap. 234 is the Trade Disputes Act (Industrial Court awards), not the Civil Procedure Act.

Bail ruling (no paras): CPC s.123 bar on bail for capital offences void under Art 2(4) 'to the extent of the inconsistency': 'S. 123(2) cannot be used as a basis to deny any suspect bail'. Own reasoned holding, though no formal declaration in the orders (bail granted).
Para 27 'section 45(3) declared invalid to the extent of its inconsistency'; formal orders para 34(b)-(c) 'declaring section 45(3) of the Employment Act 2007 invalid'.
Para 49: 'I find that the provisions of section 38 and 40 of the Civil Procedure Act ... are consistent with the Bill of Rights' (only O.22 r.7(1) CPR struck, para 51).
Para 49: same holding covers s.40 CPA: 'section 38 and 40 of the Civil Procedure Act ... are consistent with the Bill of Rights'.
Para 74 order (a): 'A declaration is hereby issued that Section 84D of KICA is unconstitutional and invalid.'

Para 118 order 1: 'To the extent that the Sexual Offences Act prescribe minimum mandatory sentences, with no discretion ... such sentences fall foul of article 28'. Order is SOA-wide (not s.8 by name) but s.8 minimums are the core; could be argued read_down given 'at liberty to impose sentences prescribed'.
Para 162(a): 'sections 158, 159 & 160 of the Penal Code are not inconsistent with articles ...'. Note orders (g) and (j) also narrow/criticise these sections (possible extra read_down event).
Para 162(a): same declaration covers s.159.
Para 162(a): same declaration covers s.160.

Para 42-43: applying Opoya construction to s.275: 'does not impose a mandatory minimum sentence, and the sentencing court has the discretion to impose a lesser sentence'; trial court 'misconstru[ed] the provisions of section 275'.
Para 180(b): 'section 21(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code must be read to permit the use of firearms, if need be, and only in the circumstances ...'.
Para 105: 'section 26 of the Sexual Offences Act is constitutional and does not violate or limit the rights of persons living with HIV'; petition dismissed para 109.

Para 19: 'I would reiterate the finding of the court in the case of Njoroge Mungai v Republic [2017] eKLR' - restates an earlier construction of s.7 to dismiss a defective-charge ground; no new holding (headnote does present it as a holding, so borderline).

Para 4-6: resentencing petition; para 4 wording copied from Maingi, then 'it is now well settled that a sentence of life imprisonment is unconstitutional' (citing Manyeso). No declaration in orders (para 7-9 resentence to 40 years).

Para 77: 'alive to the fact that this court has through several rulings found this provision as unconstitutional ... I am in agreement with Mativo, J ... A.O.O' - follows AOO, no own declaration; orders are a detention direction (para 82).

Para 22-24: follows SC Mwangi; petition 'having not met that threshold required for a finding of the unconstitutionality' - court declines to adjudicate validity. Also petitioner was convicted under Penal Code s.145(1) (para 1), not SOA s.8.

Para 77-78: 'Guided by the above decision [Akhonya], I affirm the life imprisonment sentence ... with a rider that the same life imprisonment amounts to 30 years' - sentencing following CA; para 76 even calls s.20(1) mandatory.

Para 4-5: restates SC Mwangi 'that the mandatory minimum penalties provided for under the Sexual Offences Act are lawful and not unconstitutional'; 'I find no reason to interfere with lawful sentence' - revision refused, no own holding.

Para 22: 'These decisions are binding on the High Court ... the proper course ... is to take it that life sentence is unconstitutional' - applies CA (Manyeso/Ayako) as binding; orders para 30 are resentencing only.

Para 12-13: court 'is unable to declare it unconstitutional' for want of full argument (per SC Mwangi); 'the sentence of imprisonment for life is upheld' refers to the sentence, not a constitutional finding on s.8(2).

Para 14: 'section 46 of the Kenya Broadcasting Corporation Act is in violation of Article 48 ... unconstitutional to that extent' - holding is on KBC Act s.46 (notice requirement), not CPA s.3A (only cited as the motion's basis, para 1).
